value:
The loss comes from auto-commit: enable.auto.commit defaults to true and commits the consumer's position in the background, whether or not the work handed to the pool has reached Postgres. The drained pod was killed with INSERTs still queued, the group resumed after them, so lag was 0 and 37 invoices were never written.
1. Set enable.auto.commit=false and commit offsets yourself, synchronously.
2. Simplest correct loop, without the pool: take a batch from the consumer, write it to Postgres in one database transaction with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (invoice_id) DO NOTHING, commit that transaction, and only then commit the batch's Kafka offsets. The committed offset is the next record to read: last written offset + 1 per partition. A crash between the two commits only replays the batch, and the unique invoice_id absorbs the duplicate.
3. If you keep the pool for throughput: per partition, track which offsets have committed in Postgres and commit only up to the highest offset below which every record is done, + 1, never past a gap. When partitions are revoked, wait for their in-flight INSERTs and commit their finished offsets before the revocation completes, so the next owner repeats little.
A rebalance then cannot lose an invoice: anything not committed is delivered again, and the ON CONFLICT clause makes the replay harmless.
reason: The old reference asserted confluent-kafka API names (Consumer, consume(num_messages=..., timeout=...), commit(asynchronous=False), on_revoke) and a made-up db.transaction(); no Python client is pinned (sources.yaml has none), so per the brief's rule 6 they go. value: Per second, with leaders spread evenly over the zones: producers reach a leader in another zone 2/3 of the time, about 100 MB/s; the four consumer groups fetch from leaders, 2/3 of them in another zone, 4 x 150 x 2/3 = about 400 MB/s; replication sends each byte to two followers, up to 2 x 150 = 300 MB/s across zones (exactly that once every partition has one replica per zone; today it depends on the placement). So today up to about 800 MB/s, about half of it consumer fetches. Remove that half with follower fetching, in this order: 1) broker.rack=<zone> on every broker (read-only, rolling restart); 2) find partitions without a replica in every zone (kafka-topics.sh --describe) and reassign them with throttled kafka-reassign-partitions.sh plans, because setting broker.rack does not move existing replicas; 3) replica.selector.class=org.apache.kafka.common.replica.RackAwareReplicaSelector on the brokers (read-only, rolling restart); 4) client.rack=<zone> on every consumer. Consumers then read from the in-zone replica and fall back to the leader when there is none. Result about 400 MB/s (100 produce + 300 replication); if some followers now share their leader's zone, step 2 adds a little replication traffic. Do not lower the replication factor: replication is the price of surviving a zone loss. Trade-off: a follower serves records only after it has them, so end-to-end latency rises; how much that matters depends on your consumers' latency budget, which you did not give, nor the price per GB.
reason: The old reference stated today's replication as 300 MB/s and the total as 800 MB/s; with broker.rack unset and arbitrary placement (the question), some followers may share their leader's zone, so today's replication is at most 300 MB/s and step 2 can raise it. value: Most of the bill is consumers fetching from leaders: four groups x 150 MB/s x 2/3 cross-zone is about 400 of the up to roughly 800 MB/s that crosses zones (the rest is about 100 MB/s of produce traffic and up to 300 MB/s of replication, depending on today's placement). Enable fetch-from-follower: broker.rack per zone on all brokers, RackAwareReplicaSelector as replica.selector.class, client.rack on consumers. Before switching consumers, make sure every partition has one replica per zone, reassigning those that do not, because racks only guide placement when replicas are created or moved. Expect total cross-zone traffic near 400 MB/s. Consumers will lag a little behind leader reads, so confirm the latency budget first.

value: In-place resizing gave the containers 16Gi, but a running JVM never sees in-place memory changes, so the heap is still the 4 GiB chosen at start (half of 8Gi). Even a restart would only reach Strimzi's default cap of 5 GB, because no jvmOptions are set. Put -Xms and -Xmx (for example 6g to 8g) into jvmOptions of the node pool, keeping well under 16Gi, and accept that the brokers must restart for it to apply. Broker 5 has not been resized at all: the kubelet marked the resize Deferred for lack of node capacity, and the wait-for-deferred annotation tells Strimzi to wait instead of rolling. Remove strimzi.io/in-place-resizing-wait-for-deferred from the Kafka resource so that Strimzi falls back to a rolling update of that pod, which then starts with the new resources.

value: As written the PR asks Kubernetes to shrink the 2000Gi claims to 800Gi, which it does not support; only growth is possible in place. Deleting each broker's PVC with strimzi.io/delete-pod-and-pvc would throw data away on purpose; that annotation is a last resort for broken storage. With Cruise Control you can shrink inside the existing pool instead: revert the change to volume 0 and add a second JBOD volume to the brokers pool, id 1, persistent-claim, size 800Gi, class st1. Then create a KafkaRebalance with mode remove-disks and moveReplicasOffVolumes listing brokerId 0 to 5, each with volumeIds [0]; wait for ProposalReady, approve it and wait for Ready. Only after that remove volume 0 from the pool (the KRaft metadata log then moves to volume 1, which rolls the brokers) and delete the old 2000Gi PVCs yourself, since deleteClaim is false. value:
Layout: one Kafka cluster and one namespace, for example kafka-tenants, holding every team's KafkaTopic and KafkaUser resources. The Entity Operator's Topic and User Operators each watch a single namespace for a single cluster, so they cannot serve 15 team namespaces. Self-service then means each team owns a directory in a GitOps repository that syncs into that namespace, with review rules per directory. A team that needs full independence gets its own cluster.

Isolation: enable simple authorization in the Kafka resource (spec.kafka.authorization type simple); today the brokers enforce no ACLs, and the KafkaUsers' authorization type must match the cluster's. Every listener the teams use needs authentication (scram-sha-512 or tls), so each client is its own KafkaUser. Give each team a prefix such as team-a. and KafkaUsers whose ACLs use patternType: prefix on topics and consumer groups starting with it. Do not turn on allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found.

Noisy neighbours: set spec.quotas on each team's KafkaUsers (producerByteRate, consumerByteRate, requestPercentage), tighter for the two batch teams.

Size: 15 x 40 x 12 = 7,200 partitions; with replication factor 3 that is 21,600 replicas, about 3,600 per broker on 6 brokers. Check that against your broker sizing, or cap partitions per team.

Missing numbers: each team's peak produce and consume throughput and its retention, which set the broker count, disk size and quota values.

value:
The 4 tasks waited for their departed worker. cdc-connect uses incremental cooperative rebalancing (the default). When a worker leaves the group, Connect waits scheduled.rebalance.max.delay.ms, 300000 ms (5 minutes) by default, for it to return; until then its connectors and tasks stay UNASSIGNED, however idle the other workers are. Pod cdc-connect-connect-2 left at 10:02, so its tasks were reassigned at about 10:07, and the pod's return at 10:11 caused the second rebalance. The HTTP 409 at 10:04 is how Connect answers a restart request while a rebalance is in progress; no restart was needed.

Confirm from what you have: the tasks moved at about 10:07, five minutes after the pod left at 10:02 and four minutes before it came back, which is exactly the default delay, and spec.config sets no scheduled.rebalance.max.delay.ms, so the default applies. The status API showed the tasks as UNASSIGNED, not FAILED, during the gap, and the worker logs show the rebalance at about 10:07. FAILED tasks would need a restart; unassigned ones do not.

Change: lower the delay in the KafkaConnect resource, for example spec.config: scheduled.rebalance.max.delay.ms: 60000. Strimzi passes it to the workers (it is not one of the forbidden prefixes) and rolls the pods to apply it. Trade-off: a worker that returns within the delay, as in a rolling update, gets its tasks back in full; with a shorter delay, short pod restarts move tasks to other workers and back. Do not switch to connect.protocol=eager: it stops and restarts all connectors and tasks on every rebalance.
reason: Removes the connector-unassigned-task-count claim (semantics not settled by connect_metrics.html:99) and gives the timing confirmation of the new m5.

value: Under the default cooperative protocol, Connect keeps a departed worker's tasks unassigned for scheduled.rebalance.max.delay.ms (5 minutes unless set) so that a worker that comes back quickly takes them back; only then are they given to the others. The 409 was your restart request arriving during the rebalance. To check: the tasks moved five minutes after the pod left and before it returned, which is the default delay, and your spec.config does not override it; the status API showed them UNASSIGNED, not FAILED. Fix: add scheduled.rebalance.max.delay.ms: 90000 (or what your SLO allows) under spec.config of KafkaConnect cdc-connect. Pick a value above your normal pod restart time, because a worker that is away longer than the delay loses its tasks to the others during every rolling update. Eager mode is not an answer: it restarts every task on every rebalance.

value: Strimzi 1.3.1, Kafka 4.3, Argo CD 3.6.1. After a warehouse restore, our sink connector warehouse-sink (KafkaConnector in namespace data, KafkaConnect etl-connect) must replay partition 3 of topic orders from offset 1250000. The KafkaConnector is in Git (with spec.state: running) and deployed by the Application connect-prod, which our ApplicationSet connect-apps generates with automated sync, prune and selfHeal. An hour ago the on-call created a ConfigMap by hand, ran kubectl edit to set spec.state: stopped and spec.alterOffsets, and annotated the connector. The connector is running again, the annotation is still there, and the warehouse shows no replayed rows. They then ran argocd app set connect-prod --self-heal=false and tried again, with the same result. argocd app history connect-prod shows an automated sync within a minute of each kubectl edit. value:
Argo CD put the connector back. connect-prod has automated sync with selfHeal, so a live change that differs from Git is synced back: your kubectl edit set spec.state: stopped and spec.alterOffsets, and within a minute Argo CD restored spec.state: running, the value in Git (alterOffsets, which Git does not manage, stayed, as your output shows). Offsets can only be altered while the connector is stopped, so the alter never ran and the annotation is still waiting. argocd app set --self-heal=false did not help because connect-prod is generated by the ApplicationSet connect-apps; a change to a generated Application's spec.syncPolicy does not stick. The ConfigMap is also wrong: Strimzi reads offset changes from the key offsets.json, and yours is offsets.

Do it through Git:
1. Fix the ConfigMap key to offsets.json (keep the sink format: kafka_topic, kafka_partition, kafka_offset).
2. Commit spec.state: stopped and spec.alterOffsets.fromConfigMap.name: warehouse-sink-offsets on warehouse-sink and let Argo CD sync; check that the connector is STOPPED.
3. kubectl annotate kafkaconnector warehouse-sink strimzi.io/connector-offsets=alter --overwrite -n data. The annotation disappears when the update succeeds.
4. Verify: add spec.listOffsets.toConfigMap, annotate with strimzi.io/connector-offsets=list and check partition 3 shows 1250000.
5. Commit spec.state: running and remove alterOffsets.

Do not delete connect-prod or the ApplicationSet to stop the reverts: with default settings that deletes the KafkaConnect and connectors too.

value:
Use the emit-on-close strategy instead of suppress; it keeps the window results in the RocksDB-backed store. On the windowed stream, before count(), call emitStrategy(...) with the "emit on window close" strategy (KIP-825):

events.filter((k, v) -> v.result() == Result.FAILED)
      .groupBy((k, v) -> v.userId(), Grouped.with(Serdes.String(), authEventSerde))
      .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(5), Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
      // emitStrategy(<emit on window close>) here
      .count()
      .filter((wk, count) -> count >= 5)
      .toStream()
      .map((wk, count) -> KeyValue.pair(wk.key(), String.valueOf(count)))
      .to("login-alerts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()));

TimeWindows.of and grace() no longer exist in 4.x; ofSizeAndGrace replaces them. With the emit strategy the count is emitted once per window after it closes, so the filter sees only final counts. key() unwraps the windowed key. Closing depends on stream time (window end plus 1 minute grace), and stream time moves only when records arrive.
